Questions.Text: True or false: All living organisms carry out the eight life processes known as MRS C GREN.
Questions.Explanation: MRS C GREN stands for Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Cells, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition - every living organism does all eight.

Questions.Text: True or false: Fire meets all eight criteria of MRS C GREN and should be classified as a living organism.
Questions.Explanation: Fire only meets about 4 of the 8 criteria (movement, sensitivity, and some growth/reproduction). It has no cells, doesn't truly respire, excrete, or get nutrition.

Questions.Text: Which letter in MRS C GREN stands for the removal of waste products made inside the body's cells?
Questions.Explanation: E stands for Excretion - the removal of metabolic waste products produced inside cells, such as exhaling CO₂ or sweating.

Questions.Text: True or false: Plants **do not** carry out all eight MRS C GREN life processes because they cannot move.
Questions.Explanation: Plants do carry out all eight processes. They exhibit localised movement (e.g., growing toward light) even though they don't move their whole body from place to place.

Questions.Text: True or false: Water scores 2 out of 8 on the MRS C GREN criteria.
Questions.Explanation: Water can show movement and sensitivity but fails the other six criteria (no cells, no respiration, no growth, no reproduction, no excretion, no nutrition).

Questions.Text: True or false: Cellular respiration only happens when an organism is physically active.
Questions.Explanation: Cellular respiration takes place constantly in every cell of every living organism. If a cell stops respiring it will eventually die.

Questions.Text: What is the correct word equation for cellular respiration?
Questions.Explanation: $\text{Glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy}$. This is the opposite of photosynthesis.

Questions.Text: True or false: Bacteria carry out cellular respiration only in their mitochondria.
Questions.Explanation: Bacteria don't have mitochondria. Their cellular respiration takes place only in the cytoplasm.

Questions.Text: True or false: Photosynthesis (not cellular respiration) provides energy for life processes in plants.
Questions.Explanation: Photosynthesis creates glucose, but it is cellular respiration that breaks down that glucose to provide energy for life processes.

Questions.Text: In which part of an animal cell does cellular respiration mainly take place?
Questions.Explanation: Cellular respiration in animal cells mainly takes place inside the mitochondria and in the cytoplasm.

Questions.Text: True or false: Plant cells and animal cells both contain a nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, and mitochondria.
Questions.Explanation: These four structures are found in both plant and animal cells. Plant cells additionally have a cell wall, large vacuole, and chloroplasts.

Questions.Text: True or false: Chloroplasts are found in both plant cells and animal cells.
Questions.Explanation: Chloroplasts are only found in plant cells (and some other photosynthetic organisms). Animal cells do not photosynthesise and therefore do not have chloroplasts.

Questions.Text: What is the function of the cell membrane?

Options.Value: To control what goes in and out of the cell

Questions.Explanation: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell - acting as a selective barrier.

Questions.Text: True or false: Animal cells have a large permanent vacuole for storing water and nutrients.
Questions.Explanation: Only plant cells have a large permanent vacuole. Animal cells may have small, temporary vacuoles.

Questions.Text: Why do plant cells have chloroplasts but animal cells do not?

Options.Value: Animals make their own food using mitochondria
Plants need chloroplasts to carry out photosynthesis to make their own food
Animal cells are too small to fit chloroplasts

Questions.Explanation: Plants are producers - they make their own food via photosynthesis, which takes place in the chloroplasts. Animals consume food rather than making it.

Questions.Text: True or false: Photosynthesis is the reverse reaction of cellular respiration.
Questions.Explanation: In photosynthesis, CO₂ + water → glucose + oxygen (using light). In respiration, glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water + energy. They are essentially opposite reactions.

Questions.Text: Which green pigment in plant cells absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis?
Questions.Explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in chloroplasts that captures light energy to power photosynthesis.

Questions.Text: True or false: Photosynthesis can occur in darkness if the plant has enough carbon dioxide and water.
Questions.Explanation: Photosynthesis requires light energy (photo = light). Without light, the reaction cannot take place.

Questions.Text: What are the two products of photosynthesis?
Questions.Explanation: Photosynthesis produces glucose (food for the plant) and oxygen (released as a by-product through the stomata).

Questions.Text: True or false: In the Elodea experiment, the bubbles produced by the plant represent oxygen gas being released during photosynthesis.
Questions.Explanation: When Elodea photosynthesises, it releases oxygen as a by-product. This oxygen forms the bubbles we can observe and count.

Questions.Text: True or false: Transpiration is the process by which plants gain water through their leaves.
Questions.Explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water from leaves through the stomata via evaporation. Plants absorb water through their roots, not their leaves.

Questions.Text: Which environmental condition would **increase** the rate of transpiration?
Questions.Explanation: Strong wind speeds up evaporation from the leaf surface, increasing the rate of transpiration. High humidity, low temperature, and still air all slow transpiration.

Questions.Text: True or false: If a plant loses too much water through transpiration, its rate of photosynthesis will slow down.
Questions.Explanation: Water is a reactant in photosynthesis. If too much water is lost through transpiration and cannot be replaced, less water is available for photosynthesis, slowing growth.

Questions.Text: True or false: Larger leaves lose water more quickly than smaller leaves because they have more stomata.
Questions.Explanation: Larger leaves have more stomata, providing more openings through which water can evaporate into the air.

Questions.Text: What is the name of the tiny pores in leaves through which water evaporates during transpiration?
Questions.Explanation: Stomata are small openings (pores) found mainly on the underside of leaves. Water diffuses out through them during transpiration.

Questions.Text: True or false: Reforestation helps reduce the amount of CO₂ in the atmosphere by planting trees that absorb it.
Questions.Explanation: Trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis, acting as carbon sinks and reducing greenhouse gas levels.

Questions.Text: True or false: Planting non-native trees is always better for New Zealand's ecosystem because they grow faster.
Questions.Explanation: While non-native trees grow faster, they often don't support New Zealand's native wildlife. Native trees have co-evolved with local birds and insects that depend on them for food.

Questions.Text: Which of the following is **not** a benefit of reforestation?
Questions.Explanation: Reforestation reduces greenhouse gases (trees absorb CO₂). It does not increase them. The other options are all genuine benefits of reforestation.

Questions.Text: True or false: Tree roots help prevent soil erosion by holding soil in place.
Questions.Explanation: Tree roots bind the soil together, preventing it from being washed away by rain - keeping the land healthy for both plants and animals.

Questions.Text: Which plant structure is responsible for absorbing water and nutrients from the soil?
Questions.Explanation: Roots absorb water and dissolved nutrients from the soil and also anchor the plant in place.

Questions.Text: A seedling was @{a} cm tall. After two weeks it was @{b} cm tall. What is the percentage increase in height?
A plant had @{c} leaves. After a dry spell, it lost @{d} leaves. What is the percentage decrease?
True or false: Increasing by 10% then decreasing by 10% results in the original value.
Questions.Explanation: Increasing by 10% means multiplying by 1.10, then decreasing by 10% means multiplying by 0.90. Overall, the value is multiplied by $1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99$, which is less than the original value.

Questions.Text: A sunflower was @{a} cm tall on Monday and @{b} cm tall on Friday. What is the percentage increase?.
A grapevine was @{a} cm long. After pruning it was @{b} cm. What is the percentage change?
In the Elodea experiment, what is the independent variable?

Options.Value: The number of bubbles per minute
The distance of the lamp from the plant

Questions.Explanation: The independent variable is what you deliberately change. In this experiment, the lamp distance is changed to see how it affects the rate of photosynthesis.

Questions.Text: True or false: In the Elodea experiment, as the lamp moves further away, the number of bubbles per minute should increase.
Questions.Explanation: As the lamp moves further away, light intensity decreases, so photosynthesis slows and fewer bubbles are produced per minute.

Questions.Text: True or false: Using the same size piece of Elodea in every trial is an example of a controlled variable.
Questions.Explanation: Controlled variables are kept the same so they don't affect the results. Using the same size Elodea ensures differences in bubble count are due to light distance only.
